# TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference

Han Li    Lingxiang Hu    Jiacheng Huang    Ziqian Jiang    Jingkai Luo
   Wei Gao    Yunfan Tan    Zun Wang    Jiaheng Liu Affiliation: \[
Affiliation: \[ Affiliation: \[

October 8, 2026

###### Abstract

Large language model (LLM) coding agents have advanced test generation
across diverse programming tasks. However, the common practice of
evaluating tests against a single reference solution overlooks
alternative valid implementations and can overstate test quality. We
introduce TestPrism, comprising 300 test tasks from 17 sources and 3000
candidate implementations, evenly split between valid and invalid
solutions. Its primary metric, Joint Success Function, requires the
generated tests to fail on the initial program state, accept every valid
candidate, and reject every invalid candidate. Across fourteen baseline
coding agent configurations, Joint Success Function reaches only 28.00%,
whereas single reference success reaches 59.67%. Our analysis reveals
missed behaviors, unsupported assertions, and faulty test construction.
To address these weaknesses, we introduce TestHelix, which combines
heterogeneous synthesis of test and repair pairs with peer cross
validation and recursive self improvement (RSI). Across two models,
TestHelix improves Joint Success Function by 8.67 to 9.00 percentage
points over the native harness comparators in the TestHelix evaluation.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Codex and Claude Code,
can navigate repositories, modify implementations, and validate changes
through execution feedback ([Yang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib52); [Wang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib46); [Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib47); [Pan
et al., 2026](#bib.bib32); [Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib24)). These
capabilities also support automated test generation and
improvement ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib7); [Alshahwan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3)). Reliable tests must generalize across valid
implementations while remaining sensitive to specification
violations ([Zhu et al., 1997](#bib.bib58); [Barr et al.,
2015](#bib.bib5)).

##### Limitations of Existing Benchmarks.

Test generation benchmarks span function level tasks, as in TestEval
([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib45)), and repository issues, as in SWT
Bench ([Mündler et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)). A common success criterion
remains single reference evaluation: a suite must fail on the initial
program and pass on one gold solution ([Mündler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30); [Ahmed et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). Yet a requirement
can admit multiple valid implementations and plausible incorrect ones. A
test can pass this check while missing required behavior ([Qi et al.,
2015](#bib.bib36); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib27)) or imposing
unnecessary implementation constraints. We therefore ask: How robust is
the evaluation of generated tests to variation across implementations?
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
compares existing benchmarks; counting conventions and target mappings
appear in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Benchmark Comparison Conventions ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

##### TestPrism: Beyond Single Reference Evaluation.

TestPrism contains 300 test tasks from 17 sources across six programming
languages, covering repository maintenance, algorithmic programming, and
performance optimization. We adapt executable tasks to a shared
interface, enrich their candidate patch sets, verify and select diverse
implementations, and convert the tasks for test generation. For each
test task, we retain the reference and select four valid alternatives
and five invalid implementations through explicit diversity checks.
Building on this pipeline, we construct TestPrism with 2,000 tasks from
17 source benchmarks, partitioned into 1,700 training tasks and 300 test
tasks. The test set contains 3000 candidate implementations and spans
six task categories and 34 subcategories across 67 repositories and
projects. This task diversity supports assessing how well coding agents
generalize test generation across programming scenarios. The disjoint
training set supports adapting test generation strategies in TestHelix’s
recursive self improvement (RSI) stage.

Our evaluation protocol executes each submitted suite on the initial
state and every candidate. Its primary metric, Joint Success Function,
requires initial failure and agreement with every candidate label.
Restricting the panel to the reference recovers single reference
evaluation as a minimal approximation. Complementary acceptance,
rejection, and coverage metrics locate behavioral disagreements and the
code exercised by the tests.

##### TestHelix.

We introduce TestHelix to address these weaknesses through heterogeneous
synthesis of test and repair pairs. Its inner workflow establishes
consistency within each pair, then uses peer cross validation,
comprising cross execution, semantic review, and corrective feedback, to
check and correct tests across pairs. Its outer RSI loop proposes test
generation strategies on training tasks and validates one frozen
challenger on a disjoint set before benchmark evaluation.

##### Takeaways.

We evaluate fourteen coding agent configurations spanning six model
families. Our analysis reveals four key findings: ❶ Reliable test
generation remains far from solved by frontier models. The strongest
baseline reaches only 28.00% Joint Success Function, compared with
59.67% single reference success
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).
Coverage tracks success: change and entry coverage correlate with Joint
Success Function across configurations ($`r=0.91`$ and $`0.96`$).
❷ Joint Success Function is a dynamic measure of reliability across
implementations. Larger candidate panels impose additional behavioral
requirements, as shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
Single reference evaluation is its weakest special case and an upper
bound on expanded panel success. ❸ Failures span coverage gaps, faulty
checks, and execution logic errors. We sample 300 failed trajectories,
50 from the highest Joint Success Function configuration in each of six
model families, and analyze 286 after excluding 14 timeout trajectories.
The category shares among the analyzed trajectories are 34.6%, 50.0%,
and 15.4%, respectively
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")),
explaining limited reliability through omissions, misjudgments, and
execution failures. Missing inputs and weak assertions can pass single
reference evaluation while accepting invalid patches. ❹ Heterogeneous
synthesis helps tests generalize across implementations. With peer cross
validation using diverse repairs to check and correct tests and RSI
adapting test generation strategies across tasks, TestHelix raises Joint
Success Function over Single by 11.67 to 12.00 percentage points under
matched inference budget caps
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).

##### Contributions.

Our work makes three contributions:

- •
  We construct TestPrism, with 1,700 training tasks and 300 test tasks
  from 17 sources, providing 3000 labeled implementations for
  evaluation. Its Joint Success Function criterion extends single
  reference evaluation to assess whether generated tests accept valid
  alternatives and reject incorrect implementations.
- •
  We evaluate fourteen coding agent configurations across six model
  families and develop an error taxonomy from 286 retained failed
  trajectories spanning their highest Joint Success Function
  configurations. These complementary analyses characterize current
  agent performance and identify specific mistakes that cause generated
  tests to miss invalid behavior or reject valid alternatives, including
  failures hidden by single reference evaluation.
- •
  We introduce TestHelix, which combines heterogeneous synthesis with
  peer cross validation and RSI. It checks and corrects tests through
  cross execution and semantic review, and adapts reusable test
  generation strategies to improve reliability across implementations
  under matched inference budget caps.

## 2 TestPrism

To evaluate whether generated tests generalize beyond a single
reference, we construct TestPrism through four steps: (i) task screening
and adaptation, (ii) task selection, (iii) patch generation and
validation, and (iv) diversity filtering and task conversion. Each test
instance pairs a test generation task with a curated panel of valid and
invalid implementations.
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 TestPrism ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
outlines the pipeline.

![Refer to caption](2610.12289v1/testprism_overview.png)

Figure 1: Overview of TestPrism construction and evaluation.

### 2.1 Step 1: Task Screening and Adaptation

We curate tasks from 17 public benchmarks, including the widely used SWE
bench and Terminal Bench families ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib15);
[Merrill et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), requiring traceable test provenance
and documented validation
(Appendix [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Source Test Validation ‣ B.3 Patch Generation and Validation ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).
We retain coding tasks whose requirements can be checked with executable
tests, excluding unusable Docker images and irreproducible environments.
Adapters map tasks to Harbor’s instruction, environment, tests, and
solution components while preserving requirements, initial states,
verifiers, reference solutions, dependencies, services, and execution
limits.

### 2.2 Step 2: Task Selection

We screen tasks using Solution Size, the effective lines of solution.sh;
Test Count, the enumerated test functions or metadata checks; and Test
Density, this count per file changed by the reference solution. Lower
bounds are calibrated to each source’s own distribution, and source
quotas balance representation across the disjoint training and candidate
test sets.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Task Selection ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
reports the source-specific screening thresholds. We retain 1,700
training tasks for TestHelix’s recursive self improvement (RSI); only
candidate test tasks undergo the remaining patch generation and
filtering steps.

### 2.3 Step 3: Patch Generation and Validation

Verifier validation.  All source benchmarks provide test suites
validated through execution checks, expert review, or official
competition evaluation. Our additional validation round checks each
adapted verifier before candidate generation, requiring failure on the
initial state and success on the reference solution. Two experts use
development experience to independently assess task requirements and
source verifiers for potential overfitting and coverage gaps. Discussion
clarifies disagreements; tasks with unresolved concerns are excluded.
Independent verifier usability judgments achieve Cohen’s
$`\kappa=0.68`$.
Appendix [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Source Test Validation ‣ B.3 Patch Generation and Validation ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
documents the prior validation evidence and our additional review.

Patch generation.  We generate candidate patches with different coding
agents and models of varying capabilities to capture alternative
solutions and errors arising during task solving, complementing mutation
based fault models ([Just et al., 2014](#bib.bib16); [Jia & Harman,
2011](#bib.bib14)). We remove empty submissions, exact duplicates, and
inapplicable patches, then execute the source verifier in clean
environments and record outcomes for individual checks. A candidate is
valid if every check passes and invalid if any check fails. These labels
remain fixed when evaluating generated tests.

### 2.4 Step 4: Diversity Filtering and Task Conversion

We assemble panels of one reference, four valid alternatives, and five
invalid implementations. The valid group must meet the mean AST distance
criterion. For invalid implementations, different sets of failed
verifier checks pass the diversity check directly; matching sets require
the AST Jaccard check. We refine panels through generation and
replacement until both group criteria hold, then apply source quotas in
final sampling.

The test generation adapter converts each programming task into a test
authoring contract: submit tests, fixtures, and one executable entry
script in a designated artifact directory. The original requirement
defines the behavior to test; the candidate panel remains hidden during
test generation.
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Diversity Filtering and Task Conversion ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
gives the filtering stages and implementation details.

### 2.5 TestPrism Statistics

TestPrism contains 2,000 tasks collected and adapted from 17 source
benchmarks, with 1,700 tasks in the training set and 300 in the test
set. The partitions are disjoint. The test set contains 3000 labeled
implementations across six programming languages and 67 repositories and
projects.

The sources span repository maintenance, evolved function
specifications, olympiad programming, and numerical optimization ([Xia
et al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib40); [Press
et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)).
Appendix [B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Benchmark Statistics ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
provides source and language statistics, the source test count
distribution
(Figure [5](#A2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ B.5 Benchmark Statistics ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")),
the six task categories and 34 subcategories, and counting conventions.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Task Selection ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
details partitioning procedures and eligibility criteria. The filtering
funnel appears in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Task Selection ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

### 2.6 Evaluation Protocol

We run each submitted entry script on the initial state and every panel
implementation, resetting the target each time and recording one
verdict. For task $`i`$, $`b_{i}`$ is the initial state and $`g_{i}`$
the reference; $`\mathcal{V}_{i}`$ contains $`g_{i}`$ and four valid
alternatives, and $`\mathcal{I}_{i}`$ contains five invalid candidates.
Indicators $`a_{i}(p)`$ and $`r_{i}(p)`$ denote recorded pass and fail
outcomes on $`p`$; both are zero for missing outcomes or recognized
execution errors.

Behavioral metrics.  Reference Acceptance Rate measures single reference
fail to pass success over the fixed $`N=300{}`$ tasks:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\text{Reference Acceptance Rate}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i}(b_{i})\,a_{i}(g_{i}).
``` |  |

Valid Acceptance Rate measures acceptance of valid alternatives; Invalid
Rejection Rate measures rejection of invalid candidates. For each task,
$`A_{i}`$ is the fraction of recorded valid alternatives accepted,
excluding $`g_{i}`$, and $`R_{i}`$ is the fraction of recorded invalid
candidates rejected. Let $`\mathcal{T}_{V}`$ and $`\mathcal{T}_{I}`$
contain the tasks with defined $`A_{i}`$ and $`R_{i}`$, respectively. We
average each task’s rate with equal weight:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Valid Acceptance Rate}=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{T}_{V}\rvert}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{V}}A_{i},\qquad\text{Invalid Rejection Rate}=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{T}_{I}\rvert}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{I}}R_{i}.
``` |  |

Neither rate is gated by Reference Acceptance Rate. Missing records are
excluded; recorded errors remain in the task denominators. An empty task
denominator leaves its rate undefined. All full-benchmark configurations
have complete observations, so both means cover all $`N`$ tasks
(Appendix [B.6.1](#A2.SS6.SSS1 "B.6.1 Behavioral Metric Definitions ‣ B.6 Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).
We also report their harmonic mean $`H`$, computed from both rates at
the precision shown in the tables.

Coverage.  Following SWT Bench, Change Coverage ($`\Delta\mathcal{C}`$)
measures the fraction of executable reference changes exercised by
generated tests; trusted tests identify targets in the corresponding
initial or reference state ([Mündler et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)).
Following TestExplora, Entry Coverage measures coverage of executable
code within production entry spans identified by trusted tests in the
reference state, potentially beyond changed lines ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)). Failed collection and empty denominators yield no
numeric value; we report collection counts
(Appendix [B.6.2](#A2.SS6.SSS2 "B.6.2 Coverage Collection and Aggregation ‣ B.6 Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).

Joint Success Function.  Our primary metric, Joint Success Function,
takes candidate patch sets $`\mathcal{P}=(P_{i})_{i=1}^{N}`$, where
$`g_{i}\in P_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{i}\cup\mathcal{I}_{i}`$. It
requires initial failure, acceptance of every selected valid
implementation, and rejection of every selected invalid implementation:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Joint Success Function}(\mathcal{P})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i}(b_{i})\,\prod_{p\in P_{i}\cap\mathcal{V}_{i}}a_{i}(p)\,\prod_{p\in P_{i}\cap\mathcal{I}_{i}}r_{i}(p).
``` |  |

Reference sets $`\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ref}}=(\{g_{i}\})_{i=1}^{N}`$
recover Reference Acceptance Rate. Unless otherwise specified, reported
Joint Success Function values use the full panels,
$`P_{i}=\mathcal{V}_{i}\cup\mathcal{I}_{i}`$, fixed across systems.
Joint Success Function cannot exceed Reference Acceptance Rate; their
gap measures the fraction of tasks that pass reference evaluation but
fail joint evaluation, including missing or erroneous outcomes.

## 3 TestHelix

To improve test reliability beyond a single reference implementation, we
propose TestHelix with three components
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 TestHelix ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).
Heterogeneous synthesis generates diverse test and repair pairs to
explore complementary behaviors and implementation hypotheses. Peer
cross validation checks tests against peer repairs to expose and correct
errors that agreement with one repair can miss. Recursive self
improvement (RSI) learns from execution feedback across tasks to improve
the test generation strategy.

![Refer to caption](2610.12289v1/testhelix_architecture.png)

Figure 2: TestHelix architecture.

### 3.1 Heterogeneous Synthesis

Diversity. We encourage diversity by assigning distinct exploration
strategies to isolated coding agents. Each agent independently develops
a test patch $`T_{k}`$ and a repair patch $`P_{k}`$ from public task
requirements. Internal consistency. We enforce internal consistency
within each pair by requiring $`T_{k}`$ to reproducibly fail on the
initial program and pass on $`P_{k}`$. Agents use local execution
feedback to refine their pairs until this condition holds or the budget
is exhausted.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Heterogeneous Synthesis ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
details the synthesis prompts and branch strategies.

### 3.2 Peer Cross Validation

Cross execution. We execute $`T_{i}`$ against internally consistent peer
repairs $`P_{j}`$ to expose overly restrictive tests or incomplete
repairs. Semantic review. An independent reviewer checks assertions
against public requirements without seeing generated repairs and
supports every blocking finding with public evidence. Corrective
feedback. We use reviewed counterexamples to correct the pairs. When
distinct qualified repairs pass the approved suites, we use differential
challenges to find inputs that separate them ([Yang et al.,
2011](#bib.bib54)). We repeat execution and review after revision. Suite
merging. We combine compatible suites with common passing witnesses and
validate the merged suite in a fresh environment.
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Peer Cross Validation ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
documents the review prompt and evidence boundary.

### 3.3 Recursive Self Improvement

We initialize TestHelix with a basic strategy. However, improving test
generation performance across heterogeneous tasks involves a large
semantic search space. We use RSI to refine the strategy within the
existing workflow while keeping the pair count and inference budget
fixed. We optimize Reference Acceptance Rate for a denser success
signal, since the stricter Joint Success Function can leave incremental
harness improvements unrewarded. Heterogeneous synthesis and peer cross
validation target the broader discrimination across implementations
required by Joint Success Function.

We use AutoSaddler ([Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib33)) to optimize the
harness strategy through reflective evolution. It selects a parent
strategy, diagnoses its execution traces, and proposes a revision. The
parent and child are evaluated on the same tasks using Reference
Acceptance Rate; their performance guides selection, while reflection
extracts reusable lessons for later rounds.
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Recursive Self Improvement ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
details the optimization setup.

## 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations?

To assess test reliability across implementations, we investigate the
following Research Questions (RQs): RQ1 benchmarks coding agents and
relates coverage to success; RQ2 examines how expanding diverse
candidate patch sets affects Joint Success Function; RQ3 characterizes
test generation failures; and RQ4 evaluates TestHelix and its
components. Evaluations follow the shared protocol in
Section [2.6](#S2.SS6 "2.6 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 2 TestPrism ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

### 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents

How reliably do current coding agents generate tests that distinguish
valid and invalid implementations?

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
benchmarks coding agents on all 300 tasks, reporting the highest Joint
Success Function configuration from each of six model families among
fourteen evaluated configurations. The main comparison uses native
coding agents to reflect the close coupling between model training and
harness design.
Appendix [D.1.1](#A4.SS1.SSS1 "D.1.1 Baseline Configurations ‣ D.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
provides the remaining eight configurations, including earlier versions
and model variants. We also examine how coverage and the balance between
acceptance and rejection relate to Joint Success Function across all
fourteen configurations;
Appendix [D.1.2](#A4.SS1.SSS2 "D.1.2 Metric Correlations ‣ D.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
provides the correlation analysis.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | RAR | VAR | IRR | $`H`$ | $`\Delta\mathcal{C}`$ | $`\mathrm{EC}`$ | JSF |
| Claude Fable 5.1 | 59.67% | 72.67% | 79.33% | 75.85% | 82.33% | 54.33% | 28.00% |
| Kimi K3 | 56.67% | 63.67% | 83.00% | 72.06% | 84.33% | 52.00% | 24.67% |
| Qwen3.8 Max | 54.67% | 77.00% | 66.00% | 71.08% | 80.33% | 50.33% | 23.67% |
| GPT 5.6 sol -max | 54.00% | 61.33% | 86.00% | 71.60% | 70.33% | 49.00% | 23.33% |

Table 2: Performance of the highest Joint Success Function configuration
from each model family.

Reference success often fails to extend to other implementations. Claude
Fable 5.1 leads Joint Success Function at 28.00%, compared with 59.67%
against the reference. Five of the six configurations score higher on
Invalid Rejection Rate than Valid Acceptance Rate, indicating difficulty
accepting permissible implementations. GLM 5.3 has the highest rejection
rate but the lowest acceptance and joint success rates: defect rejection
alone is insufficient. Across all fourteen configurations, the positive
association between $`H`$ and Joint Success Function supports balancing
both requirements. Change Coverage and Entry Coverage also correlate
with joint success (Pearson $`r=0.91`$ and $`0.96`$). Reaching relevant
behavior helps, but does not ensure that assertions judge it
correctly ([Inozemtseva & Holmes, 2014](#bib.bib12); [Zhu et al.,
1997](#bib.bib58)).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 4.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success

How does expanding a diverse candidate patch set affect Joint Success
Function?

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
shows Joint Success Function and candidate diversity under three patch
addition schedules. We summarize diversity using mean pairwise Jaccard
distance between AST feature sets. For this diagnostic, we randomly
sample 50 benchmark tasks and continue the candidate construction
pipeline to expand each task’s standard ten implementations to 15: the
reference, seven additional valid alternatives, and seven invalid
candidates. We keep each submitted suite fixed and grow its candidate
set from the reference repair by adding valid alternatives, invalid
candidates, or the two in alternation. The alternating schedule starts
with an invalid addition and contains eight valid and seven invalid
implementations at $`k=15`$. The diagnostic equally weights the six
model configurations in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference"),
each evaluated on the same 50 tasks. Candidate count and diversity
change together in this diagnostic;
Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
provides the construction and calculation details.

The results show two ways in which an expanded panel can remove
reference successes: tests may reject valid alternatives or accept
invalid candidates. Mean Joint Success Function starts at 49.33%,
reaches 38.10% after five valid additions and 30.49% after five invalid
additions, and reaches 24.33% after nine alternating additions. The
complete pool endpoints are 37.33%, 29.33%, and 23.33% for the valid,
invalid, and alternating schedules. The tests remain fixed while the
panel imposes additional acceptance and rejection requirements.

Figure 3: Joint Success Function and candidate diversity under three
patch addition schedules.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures

What error mechanisms occur in generated tests, and which remain hidden
under single reference evaluation?

We sample 50 failed trajectories, each with a zero task-level joint
success indicator, from each configuration in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
After excluding 14 timeouts, two experts independently annotate all 286
retained trajectories using seven error subtypes (Cohen’s
$`\kappa=0.81`$).
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
pairs the full benchmark metrics from
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
with failure mechanisms from this sample. The radar axes are
independently scaled: the displayed lower and upper bounds define the
center and outer polygon for each metric.
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
details expert annotation, disagreement resolution, and subtype
definitions.

![Refer to caption](2610.12289v1/rq3_model_profiles.png)

(a) Model profiles

![Refer to caption](2610.12289v1/error_taxonomy.png)

(b) Test failure mechanisms

![Refer to caption](2610.12289v1/rq3_model_legend.png)

Figure 4: Model profiles across all 300 benchmark tasks (a) and failure
mechanisms in 286 sampled failed trajectories after excluding 14
timeouts (b).

The profiles in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")(a)
show contrasting strengths: GPT 5.6 sol -max and GLM 5.3 reject invalid
candidates more reliably than they accept valid alternatives, whereas
Qwen3.8 Max shows the reverse. Panel (b) summarizes 99 coverage gaps
(34.6%), 143 faulty checks (50.0%), and 44 execution logic errors
(15.4%). Coverage gaps. Tests can exercise an operation while missing
the input combinations that expose a defect. A poker suite never
compares an ace low straight against three of a kind, allowing a
candidate that misclassifies the straight as a high card to pass. Faulty
checks. The largest group shows that exercising relevant behavior does
not ensure that tests judge it correctly, consistent with prior
observations of incorrect generated assertions ([Yuan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)). A bracket parser suite includes unmatched
parentheses but checks only the output count, accepting a candidate that
discards valid groups. Both the poker and bracket suites fail on the
initial program and pass on the reference, yet accept an invalid
alternative. These paired outcomes show how missing input combinations
and weak assertions can survive reference evaluation while additional
patches expose them. Execution logic errors. Errors in the tests’ own
execution can also prevent them from evaluating candidate behavior. An
EvoEval suite accesses a function stored on its test class through self,
unintentionally binding an extra argument and failing even on the
reference repair. Such failures explain broader reliability problems but
do not establish a single reference blind spot.

### 4.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix

How do heterogeneous synthesis, peer cross validation, and recursive
self improvement contribute to joint test reliability?

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
compares five TestHelix configurations for GPT 5.6 sol and Kimi K3,
alongside native agent comparators, Codex (max) and Kimi Code,
respectively. Within each model group, the TestHelix configurations
share the same base model and tools and use the same total inference cap
per benchmark task, shared across pairs. We compare single pair
generation with three heterogeneous pairs followed by random submission
of one locally qualified suite, then enable peer cross validation at
$`K=3`$ and $`K=5`$. The final configuration applies RSI at $`K=3`$
using one shared strategy optimized with Opus 4.6 on 600 training tasks
for Reference Acceptance Rate and frozen for evaluation with both
models. The other configurations retain the initial strategy.
Appendix [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
provides the experimental controls, and
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Recursive Self Improvement ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
details the strategy optimization.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Setting |  |  | GPT 5.6 sol |  |  |  |  | Kimi K3 |  |  |  |  |
| HS ($`K`$) |  PCV |  RSI |  RAR |  VAR |  IRR |  $`H`$ |  JSF |  RAR |  VAR |  IRR |  $`H`$ |  JSF |
| Native agent |  |  |  54.00 |  61.33 |  86.00 |  71.60 |  23.33 |  56.67 |  63.67 |  83.00 |  72.06 |  24.67 |
| 1 |  ✗ |  ✗ |  51.00 |  57.50 |  86.73 |  69.15 |  20.33 |  53.67 |  56.25 |  70.93 |  62.74 |  21.67 |
| 3 |  ✗ |  ✗ |  51.33 |  58.08 |  87.27 |  69.74 |  21.00 |  54.00 |  57.00 |  71.33 |  63.36 |  22.67 |
| 3 |  ✓ |  ✗ |  57.67 |  64.25 |  85.33 |  73.30 |  27.67 |  58.00 |  60.08 |  76.80 |  67.42 |  29.00 |
| 5 |  ✓ |  ✗ |  57.33 |  65.25 |  85.73 |  74.10 |  28.33 |  57.33 |  61.50 |  76.27 |  68.09 |  29.67 |
| 3 |  ✓ |  ✓ |  60.67 |  69.17 |  87.27 |  77.17 |  32.33 |  62.00 |  64.25 |  78.67 |  70.73 |  33.33 |

Table 3: Native agent comparisons and TestHelix ablations. HS denotes
heterogeneous synthesis of $`K`$ test and repair pairs; PCV denotes peer
cross validation. All scores are percentages.

Across both models, larger gains come from using the generated pairs to
improve tests than from heterogeneous synthesis without peer cross
validation. Generating three heterogeneous pairs and randomly submitting
one improves Joint Success Function by at most one percentage point over
single pair generation. Enabling the complete peer cross validation
process at the same $`K=3`$ adds more than six points, supporting the
use of alternative repair hypotheses to challenge, refine, and select
tests before submission. Expanding peer cross validation to five pairs
yields only 0.67 additional points, whereas RSI improves the three pair
process by 4.33 to 4.67 points. Under these inference caps, improving
how tests are generated and checked therefore offers a larger gain than
allocating the budget to additional pairs. The evolved configuration
achieves the highest Joint Success Function for both models and exceeds
their native coding agents, suggesting that the generation workflow
remains a useful target for improving reliability with a fixed base
model.

## 5 Related Work

Coding agents and test generation benchmarks.  SWE bench evaluates
repository changes with executable tests ([Jimenez et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15); [Yang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib53)); Terminal Bench
assesses command line tasks ([Merrill et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), and
ContextBench evaluates context retrieval ([Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib25)). SWT Bench studies tests derived from GitHub
issues ([Mündler et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)); RESTestBench evaluates
requirement based REST API tests using related mutants ([Kogler et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)). TestPrism evaluates test generation across
heterogeneous sources using fixed valid and invalid implementation
panels. TestHelix uses AutoSaddler ([Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib33)) to
search a large semantic space of test generation strategies, drawing on
Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)) and prior work on
reflective feedback and prompt optimization ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib41); [Khattab et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Yuksekgonul
et al., 2024](#bib.bib56); [Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)).

Test generation and coverage.  Randoop and EvoSuite use random
generation and search ([Pacheco & Ernst, 2007](#bib.bib31); [Fraser &
Arcuri, 2011](#bib.bib10)). Language model approaches evaluate execution
and coverage ([Schäfer et al., 2024](#bib.bib39); [Xu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib51)). CodaMOSA and CoverUp use coverage feedback to guide
generation ([Lemieux et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Pizzorno & Berger,
2025](#bib.bib34)), while SymPrompt structures prompts around execution
paths ([Ryan et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)). TestExplora studies repository
test generation and Entry Coverage ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)).
TestPrism reports task scoped coverage alongside behavioral
discrimination.

Test adequacy and executable oracles.  Mutation testing assesses
rejection of faulty variants ([Jia & Harman, 2011](#bib.bib14)). PROBE
augments repair benchmark tests with reference variants and checks
robustness under behavior preserving transformations ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib23)). Joint Success Function jointly requires acceptance
of valid and rejection of invalid candidates. The oracle problem and
patch plausibility limit executable verdicts ([Barr et al.,
2015](#bib.bib5); [Qi et al., 2015](#bib.bib36)): broader observed
behavior does not establish label completeness or semantic correctness.
CodeT selects code through agreement with generated tests ([Chen et al.,
2022](#bib.bib6)); CodeRL combines test feedback with a learned critic
to refine code ([Le et al., 2022](#bib.bib19)).

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced TestPrism to evaluate generated tests beyond a single
reference. Its Joint Success Function checks acceptance of valid
alternatives and rejection of defective implementations across diverse
candidate sets. Our evaluation reveals persistent limitations in
frontier coding agents; analysis of 286 retained failed trajectories
across six model families identifies coverage gaps, faulty checks, and
execution logic errors. TestHelix improves joint success through
heterogeneous synthesis, peer cross validation, and recursive self
improvement, supporting more reliable test generation across
implementations.

## Appendix A Benchmark Comparison Conventions

Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
compares behavioral and coverage targets: a check marks the
corresponding target, a dagger marks a related check with different
granularity or definitions, and a cross marks its absence from the main
protocol. Reference Acceptance Rate measures the fail to pass transition
from the initial program to the reference implementation.

##### Behavioral and coverage targets.

TestGenEval uses mutation testing; CLOVER and MultiFileTest evaluate
tests through execution and code coverage ([Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13); [Xu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib50); [Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib48)). Their file, block, or project coverage is distinct
from reference change and entry scope coverage. SWT Bench and TDD Bench
Verified measure changed code coverage ([Mündler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30); [Ahmed et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). OmniCode jointly
requires reference acceptance and rejection of all bad patches, while
SWE Mutation reports mutant detection ([Sonwane et al.,
2026](#bib.bib42); [Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)). These checks provide
evidence beyond one reference; acceptance of valid alternatives under
Joint Success Function is outside their scope.

##### Counting conventions.

Variants counts implementations other than the reference, including
mutants; a check indicates that variants are used but no total is
established. SWT Bench’s separate patch filtering experiment is outside
that column’s main protocol scope. TestPrism has 2,700 such variants and
300 reference solutions. Languages counts individual task implementation
languages. The 300 TestPrism tasks use Python (205), TypeScript (44),
Java (19), JavaScript (16), C++ (8), and Go (8). Scope identifies test
granularity; TestPrism spans local function and file tests, multifile
projects, and repository issues.

## Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation

This appendix follows the construction steps, benchmark statistics, and
evaluation protocol in
Section [2](#S2 "2 TestPrism ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

### B.1 Task Screening and Adaptation

Source selection and prior evidence.  We select public benchmarks with
traceable task origins and documented test validation. The [SWE
bench](https://www.swebench.com/) and [Terminal
Bench](https://www.tbench.ai/leaderboard/terminal-bench/2.0) families
maintain public leaderboards with results from multiple agent
developers. Other sources draw on community maintained Exercism
exercises, official USACO competitions, and published benchmarks for
specialized programming settings.

Task adaptation.  We retain tasks centered on code and suitable for
executable test authoring, excluding tasks with unusable Docker images
or environments that cannot be reproduced. Adapters map tasks from all
17 source benchmarks to Harbor’s instruction, environment, tests, and
solution components. Dependencies, services, and execution limits follow
each source so that its original functional and performance requirements
can be checked.

### B.2 Task Selection

##### Test set selection and eligibility.

Initial screening excludes tasks outside the code testing scope and
tasks whose environments cannot be reproduced. The selection signals in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Step 2: Task Selection ‣ 2 TestPrism ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
use effective lines in solution.sh, excluding blank and comment lines
(solution_lines); test functions enumerated from source files or
benchmark test metadata (test_func_count); and this count divided by the
number of detected modified files, with a minimum denominator of one
(test_coverage_ratio). The ratio describes test density. We apply
source-specific lower bounds calibrated to each source’s distribution.
Sources with smaller typical solutions or lower enumerated test counts
use correspondingly lower bounds, preserving their representation
alongside sources with larger values. This accounts for differences in
task granularity and verifier structure; source quotas additionally
balance the benchmark composition. After enrichment, final admission
requires applicability annotations for both $`\Delta\mathcal{C}`$ and
Entry Coverage, ten physical candidate artifacts meeting the diversity
criteria in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Diversity Filtering and Task Conversion ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference"),
and agreement between each artifact digest and its manifest.

Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Test set selection and eligibility. ‣ B.2 Task Selection ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
lists the source-specific thresholds applied during difficulty
screening. Source test counts follow the complete and partial
enumeration convention in
Appendix [B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Benchmark Statistics ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
Density uses original patch paths for 204 tasks and reference file
changes reconstructed from initial task files and build specifications
for the remaining 96. It counts distinct changed, added, or removed
files, including code, configuration, tests, and documentation;
unchanged rewrites, temporary helpers, and runtime or build outputs are
excluded.

##### Training and test split.

Tasks are normalized across sources and deduplicated before
partitioning. Difficulty screening operates within source benchmarks.
Source quotas form a training set of 1,700 tasks and a disjoint
candidate test pool. The training set is fixed at this stage; candidate
test tasks continue through verifier validation, patch generation, and
diversity filtering. We select the final 300 eligible test tasks with
proportional source quotas, retaining every source, and seed 42 for
sampling within each source. Tasks not selected for the final test set
are excluded from its statistics. Candidate test tasks undergo the
verifier checks and independent human review described in
Appendix [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Source Test Validation ‣ B.3 Patch Generation and Validation ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
before final admission.

Selection uses task properties and artifact availability, independently
of Reference Acceptance Rate, Joint Success Function, or coverage
collection success. Test set membership remains fixed when runtime
observations are missing.

Filtering funnel. 
Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Training and test split. ‣ B.2 Task Selection ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
summarizes construction from an initial pool of 15,148 source tasks. The
final dataset contains 1,700 training tasks and 300 test tasks. All
entries count tasks, including stages that assess their patch sets.
Source quota exclusions denote tasks left unselected, rather than
failures of the quality checks. After the split, the training set
remains fixed and only the candidate test pool continues through
verifier validation, initial panel assembly, and diversity refinement.
Initial assembly requires one reference, four valid alternatives, and
five invalid implementations. Tasks that exhaust the shared generation
budget before filling these quotas fail initial assembly. Tasks that
fill the quotas but still fail either group criterion when the same
budget is exhausted are excluded during diversity refinement
(Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Diversity Filtering and Task Conversion ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).

### B.3 Patch Generation and Validation

#### B.3.1 Source Test Validation

Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3.1 Source Test Validation ‣ B.3 Patch Generation and Validation ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
links all 17 sources to their test provenance and original quality
controls, including execution checks, expert review, and validation
against reference or alternative solutions.

Additional validation after adaptation.  The source benchmarks provide
the original validation; our additional validation round checks the
adapted verifiers before candidate generation. We preserve the source
verifiers during adaptation and require them to reject the initial state
and accept the reference solution before using them to label candidates.
For performance tasks, failure means the initial, unaccelerated program
misses the task’s performance requirement; passing requires an
accelerated solution that meets the original task-defined thresholds
while preserving functional correctness. Candidate labels are
established independently of the generated tests under evaluation and
remain fixed across agents.

Independent verifier review.  Before candidate generation, two experts
independently review the task requirements and source verifier, judging
whether the available information supports test authoring. Drawing on
development experience, they assess potential overfitting to the
reference and gaps in requirement coverage, including checks that could
reject valid alternatives or miss incorrect behavior. Disagreements are
discussed to clarify the concerns; any task with a remaining concern
about verifier usability is excluded. Agreement on the independent
usability judgments, before adjudication, is Cohen’s $`\kappa=0.68`$.
This review complements the source validation procedures and automatic
execution checks; retained candidate labels follow the verifier outcomes
defined in
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Step 3: Patch Generation and Validation ‣ 2 TestPrism ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

|  Source |  Test provenance |  Original quality controls |
|----|----|----|
|  [Aider Polyglot](https://github.com/Aider-AI/polyglot-benchmark) |  Community maintained Exercism suites |  Expected outputs, example implementations, and reviewed [canonical specifications](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications) support specification checks and traceability. |
|  AlgoTune |  Expert solvers, input generators, and verifiers |  Two additional contributors review each task; outputs from different solver seeds check acceptance of alternative solutions ([Press et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)). |
|  DevEval (DevBench) |  Project unit and acceptance tests |  Annotators execute reference code and supplement existing tests to improve coverage ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)). |
|  EvoEval |  Generated tasks, solutions, and augmented tests |  Authors inspect tasks and reference solutions; iterative solution agreement resolves ambiguities ([Xia et al., 2024](#bib.bib49)). |
|  Long CLI |  Tests written from requirements alone |  Tests are authored without the solution repository; initial and solution states undergo failure and regression checks followed by expert review ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)). |
|  QuixBugs |  Quixey challenge programs with passing and failing cases |  Released drivers compare buggy and corrected programs on supplied cases ([Lin et al., 2017](#bib.bib26)). |
|  SWE bench |  Developer tests from merged pull requests |  Execution requires a fail to pass transition; installation and runtime failures are filtered ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)). |
|  SWE bench Live |  Tests from issue resolving pull requests |  Validation requires a fail to pass transition and consistent results across repeated runs ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)). |
|  SWE bench Multimodal |  Repository tests for visual software issues |  Ten validation runs remove inconsistent tests; authors inspect every task for feasibility ([Yang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib53)). |
|  SWE Perf |  Repository tests for performance changes |  Selected tests pass before and after optimization; timing validation uses 20 repetitions and statistical filtering ([He et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). |
|  SWE rebench |  Test patches from resolving pull requests |  Reference patches must fix initial test failures while preserving initially passing tests ([Badertdinov et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)). |
|  SWE bench Pro |  Repository tests with human review |  Repeated runs check stability; human reviewers remove irrelevant or overly broad tests ([Deng et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)). |
|  SWE PolyBench |  Repository tests and pull request updates |  Manually configured containers check failure transitions and regression preservation, excluding untestable changes ([Rashid et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). |
|  Terminal Bench |  Contributor tests and reference solutions |  [Contribution checks](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-1/tree/d28711d0da2675d0bb1d56de45ae5df6082438a3/.github) cover specification alignment, reference success, and failure without agent actions. |
|  Terminal Bench 2 |  Contributor tests and manual reference solutions |  Three reviewers check specification, execution, and exploits, averaging three review hours per task ([Merrill et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)). |
|  Terminal Bench Pro |  Programmer authored instructions and unit tests |  Independent experts review ambiguity, false positives, reference solutions, and coverage over multiple rounds ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib44)). |
|  USACO |  Official hidden tests and editorial based reference code |  Reference solutions pass hidden tests; manual resource checks compare correct and incorrect asymptotic complexity ([Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib40)). |

Table 6: Source test provenance and prior validation evidence.

#### B.3.2 Candidate Generation and Labeling

Only the candidate test pool undergoes patch generation, using different
coding agents and models of varying capabilities to produce alternative
implementations. These runs capture multiple ways of satisfying the task
requirements and errors arising during task solving. Each candidate is
stored as a patch artifact. The admission gate removes empty submissions
and exact duplicates, then checks applicability in the adapted task
environment. The source verifier executes its checks in a clean
environment, producing a matrix of candidate outcomes. A candidate is
valid when every check passes and invalid when any check fails,
regardless of its intended correctness. We retain its provenance,
identifier, label, and digest for selection and evaluation. Each task
has a single budget of 30 generated patch outputs, shared by initial
panel assembly and diversity refinement. The existing reference does not
consume this budget. Every produced patch counts once, including patches
later rejected or not selected. No per-label generation cap or separate
refinement-round cap applies.

### B.4 Diversity Filtering and Task Conversion

AST distance.  We apply each patch to the same initial program and parse
the modified production code before and after the change with fixed
versions of Tree-sitter and the corresponding language grammars. From
AST nodes in the modified regions on each side, we extract ordered local
subtrees of depth three, counting the root as depth zero. Features
preserve node types, child order, operators, and literal types and
values. Identifiers are normalized to a common token; comments,
formatting, and source positions do not contribute features.

Let $`B_{p}`$ and $`C_{p}`$ be the resulting feature sets in the initial
and candidate states. We represent the patch by its added and removed
structural features:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{A}(p)=\bigl(\{+\}\times(C_{p}\setminus B_{p})\bigr)\cup\bigl(\{-\}\times(B_{p}\setminus C_{p})\bigr).
``` |  |

Each set depends only on the patch and the common initial program, so
its definition remains fixed across comparisons. Features are
deduplicated; repeated occurrences do not increase their weight. We use
Jaccard distance:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{\mathrm{AST}}(p,q)=1-\frac{|\mathcal{A}(p)\cap\mathcal{A}(q)|}{|\mathcal{A}(p)\cup\mathcal{A}(q)|}.
``` |  |

When both sets are empty, the distance is zero; when only one is empty,
it is one. Unresolved parse errors in the changed regions leave the
distance unavailable. Such a generated candidate cannot enter the
selected panel and still counts toward the shared 30-patch generation
budget. This measure captures local structural differences; verifier
outcomes determine behavioral labels.

Group admission criteria.  We first assemble a valid group
$`V=\{p_{\mathrm{ref}},v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}\}`$ and an invalid group
$`I=\{i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},i_{4},i_{5}\}`$. Each group contains ten
distinct unordered pairs. The valid group must satisfy

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       D(V)=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{\{p,q\}\subset V}d_{\mathrm{AST}}(p,q)>0.5.
       ```                                                                 |     |

This mean includes comparisons with the reference and between
alternatives; it is not a lower bound on every pair.

For invalid implementations, we first compare the sets of verifier
checks they fail. Different failed-check sets satisfy the diversity
check directly. Candidates with the same failed-check set must
additionally pass the AST Jaccard check. Thus, AST filtering within the
invalid group is conditional on matching failed-check sets. We impose no
cross-group distance constraint: verifier outcomes already distinguish
implementations that pass all checks from those that fail at least one.

Generation and replacement.  If either group fails its criterion, we
continue generating candidates. Each new candidate undergoes the same
applicability, deduplication, and verifier checks. Its observed label
determines the group it can enter. When the valid group has not met its
criterion, we evaluate each replacement of a nonreference member and
choose the one that maximizes $`D(V)`$, accepting it only if the mean
strictly increases. For the invalid group, replacements are assessed by
their failed-check sets, with the AST Jaccard check applied when those
sets match. The reference remains fixed, and the panel always contains
one reference, four valid alternatives, and five invalid
implementations. We stop as soon as both criteria hold or after
evaluating the thirtieth generated patch. At that limit, tasks without a
complete panel satisfying both criteria are excluded. Final source
quotas select from the eligible tasks; tasks left unselected at this
stage have passed the quality filters. Every retained artifact must
match its recorded digest.

Test generation adapter.  Conversion primarily updates task.yaml to
specify submission requirements and Dockerfile to prepare the execution
environment. The original requirement remains the behavioral contract,
and candidate patches are reserved for evaluation. Submitted tests,
fixtures, and the executable entry script reside in the designated
artifact directory.

Interpretation boundaries.  The source and difficulty composition
reflects the development collection. Requiring meaningful local
production targets for $`\Delta\mathcal{C}`$ and Entry Coverage excludes
tasks whose essential outcomes lack such targets. Candidate labels
follow the validated source task contracts, while panel diversity
follows the criteria for valid and invalid groups above. Runtime and
coverage observation counts are reported separately in
Appendix [B.6](#A2.SS6 "B.6 Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

### B.6 Evaluation Protocol

This section expands the auxiliary definitions and collection
conventions for the evaluation protocol in
Section [2.6](#S2.SS6 "2.6 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 2 TestPrism ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

#### B.6.1 Behavioral Metric Definitions

For task $`i`$, let $`o(T_{i},p)`$ denote a recorded outcome in
$`\{\mathrm{pass},\mathrm{fail},\mathrm{error}\}`$ when the submitted
entry script $`T_{i}`$ runs on implementation $`p`$. The acceptance and
rejection indicators are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i}(p)=\mathbf{1}\bigl[o(T_{i},p)=\mathrm{pass}\bigr],\qquad r_{i}(p)=\mathbf{1}\bigl[o(T_{i},p)=\mathrm{fail}\bigr].
``` |  |

Both indicators are zero when the outcome is missing or a recognized
execution error. The reference transition and full panel success
indicators are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F_{i}=r_{i}(b_{i})\,a_{i}(g_{i}),\qquad S_{i}=F_{i}\,\prod_{p\in\mathcal{V}_{i}\setminus\{g_{i}\}}a_{i}(p)\,\prod_{p\in\mathcal{I}_{i}}r_{i}(p).
``` |  |

Since $`g_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{i}`$, substituting $`F_{i}`$ into $`S_{i}`$
gives the joint criterion in the main text. The benchmark rates average
these indicators over the fixed set of $`N=300{}`$ tasks:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Reference Acceptance Rate}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}F_{i},\qquad\text{Joint Success Function}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}.
``` |  |

Let $`\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}`$ contain the other valid
candidates with recorded outcomes, excluding $`g_{i}`$, and
$`\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}`$ the invalid candidates with recorded
outcomes. The corresponding task rates are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i}=\frac{\sum_{p\in\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}}a_{i}(p)}{\lvert\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}\rvert},\qquad R_{i}=\frac{\sum_{p\in\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}}r_{i}(p)}{\lvert\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}\rvert}.
``` |  |

Complete observations give denominators of four for $`A_{i}`$ and five
for $`R_{i}`$; an empty observed denominator leaves the corresponding
task rate undefined. Let
$`\mathcal{T}_{V}=\{i:\lvert\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}\rvert>0\}`$
and
$`\mathcal{T}_{I}=\{i:\lvert\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i}\rvert>0\}`$.
The reported component rates average the defined task rates with equal
weight:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Valid Acceptance Rate}=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{T}_{V}\rvert}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{V}}A_{i},\qquad\text{Invalid Rejection Rate}=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{T}_{I}\rvert}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{I}}R_{i}.
``` |  |

Neither rate requires a successful initial-to-reference transition.
Candidates without an execution record are excluded from the
corresponding task denominator. Recorded errors remain in it even if
execution did not complete, but contribute to neither numerator. A task
with an undefined rate is excluded from that metric’s mean; an empty
task set leaves the aggregate undefined. With complete observations,
both task sets contain all $`N`$ tasks. When every included task has the
same candidate count, the task mean equals the ratio of total matching
outcomes to total candidate observations. Different task denominators
can make these two averages differ.

Every reported baseline and TestHelix configuration has complete
observations on all 300 tasks: 1,200 valid-alternative and 1,500
invalid-candidate records.

The harmonic mean $`H`$ combines the aggregate acceptance and rejection
rates:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H=\frac{2\,\text{Valid Acceptance Rate}\,\text{Invalid Rejection Rate}}{\text{Valid Acceptance Rate}+\text{Invalid Rejection Rate}}.
``` |  |

It is zero when both rates are zero and undefined when either rate is
undefined. We first round Valid Acceptance Rate and Invalid Rejection
Rate to the two decimal places shown as percentages in the tables,
compute their harmonic mean, and then round $`H`$ to two decimal places.

The harness recognizes errors such as a missing entry script or a
timeout and otherwise uses the test runner’s exit status. A nonzero exit
may reflect an assertion failure or another problem inside the script,
so interpreting a candidate disagreement requires inspecting the test
and source. This limitation also applies to a recorded failure on the
initial state.

#### B.6.2 Coverage Collection and Aggregation

We use Change Coverage from SWT Bench and Entry Coverage from
TestExplora ([Mündler et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)), with measurement defined by the execution sets
below.

For $`\Delta\mathcal{C}`$, $`C_{i}`$ contains source coordinates changed
by the reference solution and executed by trusted tests in the
corresponding initial or reference state. Coordinates include the
program state: a replaced line can contribute one target in each state.
Generated test execution in the corresponding states forms $`H_{i}`$.
Trusted test execution fixes the target denominator
$`\lvert C_{i}\rvert`$. Changed lines without an observed executable
event do not contribute to it. The metric does not separately remove
formatting edits on executed code lines.

For Entry Coverage, trusted tests identify production entry points with
a unique, auditable mapping to local source spans in the reference
state. The collector forms $`E_{i}`$ from executable coordinates in
those spans, using the union of executed and unexecuted coordinates in
the generated tests’ reference state coverage report. Generated test
execution on the reference state forms $`H_{i}^{g}`$. Trusted tests fix
the entry scope; its executable coordinates need not have been executed
by trusted tests. Overlapping entry spans count each coordinate once,
and the scope can extend beyond changed lines.

The task coverage ratios are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta\mathcal{C}_{i}=\frac{\lvert H_{i}\cap C_{i}\rvert}{\lvert C_{i}\rvert},\qquad\text{Entry Coverage}_{i}=\frac{\lvert H_{i}^{g}\cap E_{i}\rvert}{\lvert E_{i}\rvert}.
``` |  |

Every benchmark task meets both applicability rules. An empty measured
denominator or failed collector receives an explicit status and no
numeric coverage value. With valid observations for all $`N`$ tasks, the
benchmark coverages are task means:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta\mathcal{C}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta\mathcal{C}_{i},\qquad\text{Entry Coverage}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{Entry Coverage}_{i}.
``` |  |

All fourteen baseline configurations in
Tables [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
and [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ D.1.1 Baseline Configurations ‣ D.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
have 300 valid observations for each coverage metric, with no failed
collections or empty measured denominators.

#### B.6.3 Mapping Stored Metrics to Reported Quantities

The stored f2p_rate field records the single reference success indicator
$`F_{i}`$: initial failure and reference acceptance by the submitted
entry script. Reference Acceptance Rate averages this indicator over the
fixed benchmark, with missing or erroneous required outcomes receiving
no success credit. A pass on the reference alone remains an execution
record and is not a separate reported metric.

The stored valid acceptance rate includes all five valid candidates,
including the reference. The task rate $`A_{i}`$ above covers the other
four candidates for Valid Acceptance Rate. Invalid Rejection Rate
measures rejection of the invalid candidates. Both metrics first compute
each task’s rate from recorded outcomes, including recorded errors as
unmatched, and then average the defined task rates with equal weight.
This follows the task averaging convention of the stored run summaries.
The stored valid acceptance rate retains the reference, so its task rate
must be recomputed over the other four valid candidates before averaging
to report Valid Acceptance Rate. The stored balanced patch accuracy is
the arithmetic mean of the stored valid acceptance rate and invalid
rejection rate. The mutation score aliases the stored invalid rejection
rate, so it provides no additional independent observation.

Joint Success Function averages the stored task resolution indicator
over the fixed benchmark. A positive indicator requires initial failure,
acceptance of every valid candidate, rejection of every invalid
candidate, and no recorded execution error. Missing required outcomes
receive no joint success credit.

Change Coverage ($`\Delta\mathcal{C}`$) is stored in
gold_patch_coverage; the general coverage field aliases its ratio. Entry
Coverage is stored in entry_coverage. Missing or undefined coverage
values remain observation gaps rather than numeric zeros. These
correspondences are checked alongside task membership and panel identity
in the analysis artifact.

| Field | Schema default |  Schema bounds |
|----|----|----|
| guidance | Empty string |  Reusable prose, at most 2,400 characters |
| lessons | Empty list |  At most 20 lessons; at most four per explicit component |
| skillRoutes | Empty list |  At most one enabled skill or null per context, seven contexts |
| initialCandidates | 2 |  Integer from 1 to 5, no greater than the maximum |
| maxCandidates | 4 |  Integer from 1 to 5 |
| maxRounds | 2 |  Integer from 1 to 3 |
| agentSteps | 12 |  Integer from 2 to 20 |
| repairSteps | 5 |  Integer from 2 to 10 |

Table 10: TestHelix strategy fields, defaults, and schema bounds.

Controlled optimization space.  The fixed $`K=3`$ comparison sets both
candidate fields to three and excludes them from mutation. The remaining
fields allocate the existing inference budget or change reusable
guidance; the execution model and its weights, tool implementations,
base skill library, execution validator, semantic review protocol, and
total task budget stay fixed. Configuration validation imposes
additional constraints: differential challenges require at least two
rounds, cross execution, semantic review, and corrective feedback. A
single proposal changes exactly one declared strategy field. A lesson
proposal changes exactly one item while preserving all others. The host
validates the schema and rejects embedded task identifiers and code
blocks in learned prose; the reflection instructions additionally
prohibit copying solutions or hidden patches. The optimizer therefore
influences execution through bounded strategy decisions, while model
interfaces and validation remain fixed. The effect of coupling between
the optimizer and execution model on learned guidance is outside this
study’s scope.

Lessons and routing.  A lesson contains an identifier, one to eight
literal retrieval triggers, text of at most 1,000 characters, and
optional component and capability tags. Explicit components are
planning, preparation, generation, repair, and review. An update renders
the text as applicability, action, and observable verification.
Retrieval uses the public task, current phase, and host execution
checkpoint; it selects at most two applicable lessons within 1,600
characters for an agent turn, or 1,200 for planning. The seven routing
contexts are general, algorithm, framework, stateful, performance, CLI,
and visual. Routes select from the fixed enabled skill library, and
reviewer skills cannot be routed to candidate generation. An empty route
list leaves specialist loading to the agent; it does not install a
learned routing strategy.

the final test suite submitted by strategy $`\pi`$ fails on the original
program and passes on its supplied reference repair; otherwise let
$`F_{i}(\pi)=0`$. The objective is
$`\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{i\in D}F_{i}(\pi)`$, the Reference Acceptance Rate
under the evaluation protocol. A missing suite, preparation error,
timeout, or unavailable required outcome receives zero in the fixed task
denominator. Training does not optimize Joint Success Function or
inspect the hidden candidate panel. The reference is accessible only to
the host scorer, while the generator receives public task information
and bounded execution feedback. The internal three branches produce one
final submitted suite: $`K=3`$ is not three independent scoring attempts
or a pass@3 objective.

Data assignment.  The 600 optimization tasks, supplied in the supporting
materials, are partitioned into 500 proposal (training) tasks and 100
search development (validation) tasks. All task assignments use seed 42.
The proposal tasks provide execution traces for diagnosis and strategy
revision. Reference Acceptance Rate on the search development set ranks
candidates and can inform subsequent search; it is consequently an
optimization signal, not independent validation. Another 100 tasks from
the remaining 1,100 in the 1,700 task training pool form a held-out
optimization test set for release validation. These three sets and the
benchmark test set are disjoint. The assignment changes neither the task
pool nor the benchmark denominator.

AutoSaddler adaptation.  The AutoSaddler search uses Claude Opus 4.6 for
candidate selection, diagnosis and revision, and subsequent reflection
through three agent sessions. Opus 4.6 also executes TestHelix on the
proposal and development tasks, yielding one strategy search with a
fixed execution model. Its evolution DAG records parent relationships,
edits, execution outcomes, and reusable lessons. We adapt
AutoSaddler ([Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib33)) to test generation by
invoking the test generation runner in single-reference evaluation mode
and mapping each completed task to the binary score above. The
adaptation constrains proposals to the strategy schema in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference"),
checks the changed field, and rejects changes to the evaluator, tools,
task inputs, or inference caps.

Optimizer configuration.  The corresponding AutoSaddler configuration
uses train_minibatch_size=25, train_eval_attempts=1, train_epochs=1,
completed_train_iterations=20, and max_candidate_proposals=40. Both
capability_phase_iterations and capability_phase_epochs are zero;
skip_session0, monotonic_full_train_gate, the adapter’s
monotonic_train_gate, and use_merge are false. Selection, mutation, and
reflection have separate session timeouts. Optimizer calls, tokens,
failures, and elapsed time are separate resource quantities from the
generator’s inference cap.

| Setting |  Value and interpretation |
|----|----|
| Training assignment |  500 proposal tasks and 100 search development tasks |
| Completion schedule |  20 completed rounds, 25 distinct proposal tasks per round, one epoch |
| Evaluation attempts |  One final suite per task and strategy; seed 42 |
| Attempt ceiling |  40 attempts to complete 20 rounds; retries recorded separately |
| Optimizer and search execution model |  Claude Opus 4.6 for both roles |
| Session timeouts |  Selection 300 s; diagnosis and revision 1,800 s; reflection 600 s |
| Candidate health check |  60 s for strategy parsing, schema checks, and runner loading |
| Phase and selection |  Capability iterations and epochs both zero; steering only; session 0 enabled |
| Full training gates |  Both proposer and engine monotonic training gates disabled |
| Merge and release |  Merge disabled; release validation restricted to one frozen challenger |

#### C.3.4 Initial Strategy, Mutable Fields, and Inference Limits

Initial strategy.  The initial strategy eagerly requests three
candidates and keeps both candidate count fields fixed at three
throughout optimization. It uses two rounds, 12 agent steps, five repair
steps, an 18,000 token context limit, a 10,000 character tool output
limit, and a 2,048 token review output limit. Cross execution, semantic
review, and corrective feedback are enabled, with one differential
challenge step and an execution positive fallback. The 12 curated skills
remain fixed; guidance, lessons, and skill routes initially are empty.
These settings instantiate the initial strategy.

| Field or resource |  Values |
|----|----|

| agentSteps; repairSteps |  $`\{10,12,14,16\}`$; $`\{3,5,7\}`$ |
| contextTokens |  $`\{16{,}000,18{,}000,24{,}000,32{,}000\}`$ |
| toolOutputChars |  $`\{8{,}000,10{,}000,14{,}000\}`$ |
| reviewMaxOutputTokens |  $`\{2{,}048,4{,}096\}`$ |
| Textual strategy fields |  Guidance, lessons, and skill routes within the existing schema |
| Task profile caps |  48 model calls; 500,000 input and 100,000 output tokens; 900 s, further limited by public task deadlines |
| Model call concurrency |  Two shared concurrent calls |
| Per call output limits |  Generation 8,192 tokens; review initially 2,048 tokens |
| Execution and timeouts |  Two execution repeats; 120 s model timeout; 180 s test timeout |
| Transport retry allowance |  One retry, included in the shared budget and usage ledger |
````
