````math
Each proposal changes one of the nine mutable fields; a lesson update
changes one lesson while preserving the rest. The six scalar ranges in
Table [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ C.3.4 Initial Strategy, Mutable Fields, and Inference Limits ‣ C.3 Recursive Self Improvement ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
define the scalar search space. Guidance, lessons, and routes obey the
schema bounds and evidence restrictions documented in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
The lower bound of two rounds preserves the differential challenge
configuration. Increasing a component limit does not increase the shared
task cap: all generation, review, repair, and feedback calls consume the
same allowance. Provider reported usage is used when available;
otherwise accounting retains conservative reservations. The task’s
public runtime limit also applies. For an official agent limit $`T`$,
the bridge reserves $`\min(120,T/4)`$ seconds for cleanup and another 20
seconds before passing a runtime cap to the Node process. The profile
cannot override that cap: the runner’s default $`T=600`$ seconds yields
a 460 second Node limit despite the 900 second profile setting. The test
execution limit is likewise the smaller of 180 seconds and the task’s
public test timeout. All compared strategies retain the same task
deadlines. Execution repeats verify a suite’s behavior and do not grant
extra independent test generation attempts. The fixed prompts appear in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

#### C.3.5 Screening, Development Tracking, and Independent Release Validation

Each completed round evaluates a parent on 25 previously unused proposal
tasks, produces a revision, and evaluates the child afresh on those same
tasks. The screen requires a strict increase in successful
initial-to-reference transitions and zero regressions among previously
successful tasks. Only a child satisfying both conditions receives
evaluation on the 100 search development tasks. The initial strategy
receives the same development evaluation once. AutoSaddler selects the
strategy with the highest Reference Acceptance Rate on the development
set under Opus 4.6 and freezes it before release validation. After this
search, the RSI configuration in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
uses the same frozen strategy with GPT 5.6 sol and Kimi K3. Neither
benchmark model supplies feedback for strategy optimization, and the
strategy is not adapted to either model during benchmark evaluation. A
development score need not increase for a candidate to be evaluated or
retained in the search history.

The release validation protocol compares exactly one frozen challenger
with the initial strategy on the separate 100 release validation tasks,
using Opus 4.6 to execute both strategies. The promotion rule requires a
positive paired difference in Reference Acceptance Rate and a one sided
exact McNemar $`p\leq 0.05`$, with the direction fixed before
evaluation. For $`w`$ challenger only successes and $`\ell`$ initial
only successes, the test uses the upper binomial tail at $`w`$
conditional on $`w+\ell`$ discordant pairs, with probability $`1/2`$
under the null. With no discordant pairs, there is no evidence for
promotion. The protocol reports both discordant counts, both success
counts, and 95% and 99% paired bootstrap intervals from 10,000 task
resamples using seed 42. Each resample keeps the two outcomes for a task
together.

This modest validation set can lack power for small improvements.
Failure to pass the gate retains the initial strategy; the validation
results must not trigger further adaptive search on those same tasks.
The gate is separate from the benchmark scores.

Independent validation results. 
Table [13](#A3.T13 "Table 13 ‣ C.3.5 Screening, Development Tracking, and Independent Release Validation ‣ C.3 Recursive Self Improvement ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
reports the paired comparison on the 100 release validation tasks.
Reference Acceptance Rate increases from 48% to 58%, a gain of 10
percentage points. Both strategies succeed on 46 tasks and fail on 40;
the remaining 14 tasks comprise 12 new successes and two regressions.
The positive gain and one sided exact McNemar $`p=0.006470`$ satisfy the
release criterion for the frozen strategy.

| Initial | After RSI |  New successes / regressions |  One sided exact McNemar $`p`$ | 95% CI (pp) | 99% CI (pp) |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| 48/100 | 58/100 | 12 / 2 | 0.006470 | $`[+3,+17]`$ | $`[+1,+20]`$ |

Appendix [B.6.2](#A2.SS6.SSS2 "B.6.2 Coverage Collection and Aggregation ‣ B.6 Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").

### D.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
shows Joint Success Function and candidate diversity. The score equally
weights the six configurations in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
on the same 50 tasks randomly sampled from the 300 benchmark tasks using
seed 42. We use the same candidate generation and verifier validation
procedure to expand each task’s standard ten implementation panel to 15
implementations: the reference, seven additional valid alternatives, and
seven invalid candidates. These additions leave the panels used in the
baseline and TestHelix comparisons unchanged. The submitted tests and
the 50 task subset remain fixed while candidate sets grow under three
addition schedules. The valid and invalid sets in the joint criterion
are the selected diagnostic candidate sets, with the same labeling and
verdict requirements.

##### Diversity convention.

We use the AST-feature Jaccard distance $`d_{\mathrm{AST}}`$ defined in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Diversity Filtering and Task Conversion ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
For a diagnostic panel $`S`$ with at least two candidates, diversity is
the arithmetic mean of $`d_{\mathrm{AST}}(p,q)`$ over its distinct
unordered pairs; a singleton is assigned zero. For each task, we add
candidates uniformly at random without replacement from the label pool
required by the addition schedule, using seed 42. The resulting order
defines nested candidate prefixes, each retaining the reference.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: Patch Diversity and Joint Success ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")(a)
computes diversity on these realized prefixes and averages equally over
the 50 tasks. This descriptive mean includes pairs across labels. The
group admission criteria apply to standard ten-implementation panels; we
do not reapply them to intermediate diagnostic subsets. Panel (c)
re-expresses the values in panels (a) and (b), pairing them by addition
schedule and patch count $`k`$. It is a descriptive visualization
parameterized by $`k`$, rather than an estimate of the relationship
between diversity and joint success at a fixed panel size.

##### Score calculation.

For configuration $`m`$ and task $`i`$, let $`c_{im}(p)`$ indicate a
correctly recorded verdict: acceptance for a valid candidate or
rejection for an invalid one. Missing outcomes and recognized errors
give $`c_{im}(p)=0`$. Beyond the valid reference $`g_{i}`$, let
$`n_{i}^{V}`$ and $`n_{i}^{I}`$ count the available valid and invalid
candidates for task $`i`$. Let $`s_{im}^{V}`$ and $`s_{im}^{I}`$ count
configuration $`m`$’s correct verdicts in the same candidate pool, and
let $`F_{im}`$ indicate its successful initial to reference transition
on task $`i`$. Under independent uniform selection without replacement
of $`a`$ additional valid candidates and $`b`$ invalid candidates, let
$`\mathcal{P}_{a,b}`$ contain these candidates and the reference for
each task. Averaging uniformly over the six configurations and 50 tasks,
the theoretical expected joint score is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\overline{\text{Joint Success Function}}(a,b)=\frac{1}{6\cdot 50}\sum_{m=1}^{6}\sum_{i=1}^{50}F_{im}\frac{C(s_{im}^{V},a)}{C(n_{i}^{V},a)}\frac{C(s_{im}^{I},b)}{C(n_{i}^{I},b)},
``` |  |

where $`C(n,j)`$ counts subsets of size $`j`$ from $`n`$ elements, with
$`C(n,j)=0`$ when $`j>n`$. The total patch count is $`k=1+a+b`$; the
initial program is always checked and is not counted as a patch. The
calculation requires $`a\leq n_{i}^{V}`$ and $`b\leq n_{i}^{I}`$ for
every task. No task is removed as $`k`$ increases. Each of the six
configurations receives equal weight. For these expanded diagnostic
pools, $`n_{i}^{V}=n_{i}^{I}=7`$. This expression averages over all
permitted subsets. A uniformly sampled addition order yields a realized
sequence of prefixes; measurements on a finite collection of such
prefixes can differ from the exact subset expectation. The reported
score checkpoints use five valid additions ($`k=6`$), five invalid
additions ($`k=6`$), and nine alternating additions ($`k=10`$).

##### Three addition schedules.

Write $`k=1+j`$, where $`j`$ counts added candidates. The valid addition
curve uses $`(a,b)=(j,0)`$; the invalid addition curve uses
$`(a,b)=(0,j)`$, both for $`0\leq j\leq 7`$. Both retain the valid
reference. The alternating curve follows the reference with an invalid
candidate, then a valid candidate, continuing to alternate:
$`(a,b)=(\lfloor j/2\rfloor,\lceil j/2\rceil)`$ for $`0\leq j\leq 14`$.
Including the reference, its label sequence is valid, invalid, valid,
invalid, and so on. At $`k=15`$, the alternating schedule contains eight
valid and seven invalid implementations. Within each addition schedule,
the curve evaluates Joint Success Function at patch count $`k`$ under
its corresponding schedule, without repeating a candidate.

At $`k=1`$, the empty product is one and the metric equals the six
configurations’ mean Reference Acceptance Rate, denoted
$`\overline{\text{Reference Acceptance Rate}}`$. Each additional
required verdict can only preserve or remove success, so expected Joint
Success Function is nonincreasing along each schedule. Within the
expanded fifteen implementation panels, for $`0\leq a\leq 7`$ and
$`0\leq b\leq 7`$,
$`\overline{\text{Reference Acceptance Rate}}=\overline{\text{Joint Success Function}}(0,0)\geq\overline{\text{Joint Success Function}}(a,b)\geq\overline{\text{Joint Success Function}}(7,7)`$.
Mean Reference Acceptance Rate is therefore the upper bound under the
weakest criterion, and the full diagnostic panel gives the lower bound
among its subsets. This ordering does not establish a universal bound on
test quality or isolate the effect of candidate diversity selection.

Mean Joint Success Function starts at 49.33% and reaches 38.10% after
five valid additions, 30.49% after five invalid additions, and 24.33%
after nine alternating additions. The complete pool endpoints are
37.33%, 29.33%, and 23.33% for the valid, invalid, and alternating
schedules. Complete pools include all admitted candidates; comparisons
at different panel sizes impose distinct verdict requirements.

All 50 tasks remain in each configuration’s denominator. Missing or
erroneous required outcomes receive no success credit, following the
main evaluation protocol. Consequently, a decrease can reflect either a
candidate disagreement or an additional missing or erroneous required
observation.

##### Marginal acceptance and rejection.

Across the fourteen baselines in
Tables [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
and [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ D.1.1 Baseline Configurations ‣ D.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference"),
Reference Acceptance Rate exceeds Joint Success Function by 15.33 to
36.00 percentage points: 53.07% to 74.58% of reference successes fail
the joint criterion. In
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference"),
Claude Fable 5.1 leads both Reference Acceptance Rate and Joint Success
Function, yet achieves joint success on only 84 of its 179 reference
successes. Qwen3.7 Plus has the highest Valid Acceptance Rate at 81.00%
but the lowest Invalid Rejection Rate at 48.67%; GLM 5.2 has the highest
Invalid Rejection Rate at 90.33% but a Valid Acceptance Rate of 44.33%.
Their Joint Success Function values are only 19.67% and 10.00%,
respectively. Strong acceptance or rejection alone therefore does not
establish reliable discrimination across the panel. These aggregate
rates describe different behavioral profiles; they do not identify the
overlap of valid and invalid candidate failures within reference
successes. RQ1 relates coverage to reference and joint success.

### D.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures

#### D.3.1 Annotation Units

A failed trajectory has task-level joint success indicator $`S_{i}=0`$
under the evaluation protocol. Using seed 42, we sample 50 such
trajectories from the configuration with the highest Joint Success
Function in each of six model families
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")),
yielding 300 trajectories. Excluding 14 timeouts leaves 286 for expert
annotation and analysis. Each observation comprises a task, model
configuration, submitted test suite, and evaluation attempt. The
reported proportions use these 286 trajectories as their denominator: 99
coverage gaps (34.6%), 143 faulty checks (50.0%), and 44 execution logic
errors (15.4%).

The examples illustrate the mechanism definitions in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")(b)
and the behavior of individual test submissions. Disputed candidate
labels do not become evidence of an erroneous generated test solely
because the generated verdict disagrees with trusted tests.

#### D.3.2 Expert Annotation and Agreement

Two experts independently annotate all 286 retained trajectories using
the seven error subtypes defined below. They inspect task requirements,
submitted test suites, initial and reference executions, candidate
outcomes, and supporting patch evidence. Cohen’s $`\kappa=0.81`$ is
computed from these independent subtype labels before adjudication. For
each disagreement, a third expert joins both experts in discussion to
determine the final label. We aggregate the final labels into the three
parent categories reported in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
and
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Analysis of Test Generation Failures ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")(b).

#### D.3.3 Subtype Boundaries

##### Coverage Gaps.

Missing Inputs concerns omitted inputs, states, configurations, or
combinations within an exercised operation. Untested Requirements
concerns entire required behaviors or entry points without acceptance
checks.

##### Faulty Checks.

Weak Checks and Wrong Criteria distinguish insufficient checks from
incorrect or unsupported behavioral criteria. Overfitting enforces
incidental implementation details beyond the task contract.

##### Execution Logic Errors.

Fixture & API Errors concern errors in constructing test fixtures or
using APIs within the test process. Command & Parsing Errors concern
errors in the test’s command execution or output collection and parsing.
External installation, network, and container failures remain
infrastructure issues. Incorrect expectations about candidate behavior
belong to Faulty Checks.

#### D.3.4 Connection to Candidate Panel Evaluation

A direct single reference blind spot requires the same submitted suite
to fail on the initial program, pass on the reference, and accept a
candidate whose contract violation is supported by local evidence.
Missing Inputs and Weak Checks provide examples of this pattern: the
same suite passes the reference while accepting an invalid alternative.

Reference failures caused by execution logic errors or other mechanisms
cannot explain a decline conditional on reference success without
additional paired evidence. Trusted candidate labels guide witness
selection but do not establish correctness for every input. These
observations identify mechanisms consistent with the aggregate
evaluation gaps; they do not establish causal attribution for aggregate
model scores or estimate the prevalence of each mechanism across the
benchmark.

### D.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix

#### D.4.1 Experimental Controls

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 RQ4: Evaluating TestHelix ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
includes native agent comparators for each model. The baseline
comparison appears in
Tables [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ 4 Can Coding Agents Generate Reliable Tests Across Implementations? ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")
and [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ D.1.1 Baseline Configurations ‣ D.1 RQ1: Benchmarking Coding Agents ‣ Appendix D Experimental Results and Analysis ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
The following protocol defines five TestHelix configurations, denoted A
through E in table order. The first four use the initial test generation
strategy; the fifth uses a strategy improved through Recursive Self
Improvement (RSI), with three test and repair pairs. Strategies remain
frozen during benchmark evaluation. Here $`K`$ counts internal test and
repair pairs, independently of the hidden evaluation panel size.

Single.  Configuration A uses one test and repair pair ($`K=1`$), with
initial state checks, an own repair control, and self correction. Its
suite qualifies locally when it reproducibly fails on the initial state
and passes on its own repair. Peer Cross Validation is disabled.

Heterogeneous Synthesis with random submission.  Configuration B uses
Heterogeneous Synthesis to develop three pairs ($`K=3`$) with distinct
synthesis directions. Each pair is developed independently using local
execution checks for self correction. Cross execution, independent
semantic review, corrective feedback, and suite merging remain disabled.
After local correction, one suite is selected uniformly at random from
the locally qualified pairs, using seed 42 fixed before evaluation. This
configuration never enters peer cross validation, and selection uses no
hidden evaluation outcomes. A task with no qualified suite remains in
the evaluation set and receives no success credit; it is not replaced or
resampled.

Peer Cross Validation.  Configuration C retains three pairs and combines
the cross execution, semantic review, and corrective feedback operations
in
Section [3](#S3 "3 TestHelix ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
Peer repairs qualify as witnesses through local consistency checks, with
distinct lineage and source content preventing duplicate support.
Independent review interprets the task, original source, tests, and
bounded execution symptoms without seeing generated repairs. Reviewed
peer counterexamples guide correction. When distinct qualified repairs
pass the existing suites and both suites pass review, differential
challenges search for missing behavioral distinctions. Revised suites
undergo fresh execution and review. Selection uses witness support, and
compatible suites with common passing witnesses may be merged. The B to
C comparison evaluates this complete feedback process, including its
selection and merging rules.

Pair count.  Configuration D uses five pairs ($`K=5`$) with the same
peer cross validation process and initial strategy as C. The C to D
comparison varies pair count under the same total inference limit. Five
pairs appear only in this comparison, without additional random
submission or RSI configurations.

RSI.  Configuration E uses peer cross validation with three pairs and
one improved, frozen test generation strategy. AutoSaddler uses Opus 4.6
for both strategy revision and task execution during optimization;
GPT 5.6 sol and Kimi K3 then share the selected strategy for benchmark
evaluation without further adaptation. Both initialCandidates and
maxCandidates are fixed at three throughout strategy search, validation,
and benchmark evaluation. The remaining guidance and allocation fields
can evolve within the same total budget. The RSI increment compares E
with C, which uses the initial strategy at the same pair count. The
frozen strategy passes the independent Opus 4.6 release validation in
Appendix [C.3.5](#A3.SS3.SSS5 "C.3.5 Screening, Development Tracking, and Independent Release Validation ‣ C.3 Recursive Self Improvement ‣ Appendix C TestHelix: Method and Strategy Details ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference").
Benchmark tasks and their hidden panels do not enter strategy updates.

Shared controls and submission.  Within each model group, all five
configurations use the same base model, public task access, evaluator,
tools, base skill library, and total inference limits. Strategy search
uses training tasks and a disjoint validation gate; both task sets
exclude the final benchmark. Learned allocations remain subject to the
same total inference limits as the initial strategy. The budget is
shared across pairs rather than multiplied by $`K`$; all requested pairs
begin in the initial round. The run configuration comprises the planning
settings, execution repetitions, random seed, pair count, and strategy.
Disabling feedback excludes it from generation and selection, including
cached evidence and prompts. Configurations A and B require local
consistency for submission. Configurations C, D, and E also require
semantic approval; if no common peer witness is available, an approved
suite with reproducible initial failure and a passing own repair remains
eligible. Internal qualification does not provide success credit in the
hidden benchmark evaluation.

Reporting and interpretation.  All 300 tasks remain in the Reference
Acceptance Rate and Joint Success Function denominators. Valid
Acceptance Rate measures acceptance of the four valid alternatives,
excluding the reference. This rate and Invalid Rejection Rate use the
observed candidate denominator within each task and average the defined
task rates with equal weight. Coverage uses observed, nonempty
measurement denominators; missing coverage is not zero. Within each
model group, all five configurations use the same benchmark task set.
These configurations share inference limits. Inference consumption
includes every role, retry, and correction call; strategy development
and benchmark inference are distinct accounting scopes. Equal limits do
not imply equal consumed compute.

The A to B comparison evaluates the complete Heterogeneous Synthesis
design, which expands both the number of independently developed test
and repair pairs and the range of exploration directions. Guided by the
branch prompts, the LLM determines concrete task-specific directions,
including complementary behaviors and corner cases. Additional pairs
provide space to pursue these directions within the same total inference
cap. This comparison therefore measures the overall benefit of
heterogeneous expansion relative to Single. The B to C comparison
evaluates the complete peer cross validation process, including cross
execution, semantic review, and corrective feedback. The C to D
comparison measures pair count under a fixed budget, and the C to E
comparison measures RSI at fixed $`K=3`$. The RSI increment is therefore
relative to the three pair peer cross validation configuration, not the
adjacent five pair row.

## Appendix E Limitations

Reliable test generation spans a broad space of task specifications,
inputs, implementations, and execution environments. This study focuses
on one part of that problem: whether tests written by coding agents
distinguish valid and invalid implementations under fixed task
contracts. TestPrism evaluates ten labeled implementations per task, and
Joint Success Function measures joint success within these finite
candidate patch sets. The comparisons concern complete deployed agent
configurations, while the TestHelix ablations examine component
contributions within each model group. The taxonomy complements these
results by characterizing recurring failure mechanisms in 286 analyzed
failed trajectories, after excluding 14 timeouts from 300 trajectories
sampled equally from the highest Joint Success Function configuration in
each of six model families. Failed trajectories have a per-task joint
success indicator of zero. The category proportions describe the
retained sample and exclude the timeout trajectories.

Source gold tests.  We select established public benchmarks with
documented test validation, including the widely adopted SWE bench and
Terminal Bench families
(Appendix [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Source Test Validation ‣ B.3 Patch Generation and Validation ‣ Appendix B TestPrism: Construction and Evaluation ‣ TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference")).
Their original quality controls provide the foundation for task and
verifier quality. Building on this foundation, our second-stage
validation checks adapted verifiers through execution and independent
expert review for requirement alignment and potential reference
overfitting; tasks with unresolved concerns are excluded. Our scope is
evaluating generated tests across implementations under these validated
task contracts. Independently re-establishing the correctness of each
upstream benchmark is outside this study.

Panel composition and diversity.  The prevalence of valid and invalid
human patches is difficult to establish and can vary across tasks and
development settings. Our equal allocation provides a balanced
evaluation design without estimating this prevalence. The diversity
contributed by a candidate also depends on task semantics,
implementation choices, defect patterns, and its relationship to
candidates already in the panel. Consequently, a valid to invalid ratio
alone does not determine diversity, and equal counts do not guarantee
equal difficulty for acceptance and rejection. Our admission checks use
mean AST distance for the valid group and failed-check sets with
conditional AST filtering for the invalid group. They do not establish
exhaustive semantic coverage or an optimal candidate set. Jaccard
distance summarizes overlap in the chosen AST feature representation and
can differ from semantic distance; its mean over a panel need not
increase with every added patch. This work introduces Joint Success
Function and candidate patch sets with explicit diversity controls.
Optimizing the label ratio, panel size, or candidate selection is
outside its scope.

Extending evaluation to evolving specifications, broader implementation
spaces, and additional execution environments remains a direction for
future work.
````
